sources.culture.conducts: What people start out holding right, for the four conducts where a figure in this profile's own outlook speaks to it (the rest start from values alone: no figure was opened). approves_bps is the national share with 'a great deal' or 'quite a lot' of confidence, as `outlook.trust` has it (World Values Survey and European Values Study, joint wave 7, as Our World in Data publishes it; opened 2026-10-11, to confirm against the survey's tables; see sources.outlook for the country and the items). Mapping, ours: answer_tribunal and take_to_tribunal <- confidence in the courts (a person who trusts the courts approves of answering a case there and of taking a wrong to it); complain <- confidence in the civil service (writing to the town is approved where the town's officers are trusted to answer); join_union <- confidence in labour unions. Weak: confidence in an institution is not approval of an act toward it, and the share above a threshold is read as a mean, as outlook does; the figure sets where people start (their own lean and their picture of what others approve), nothing else, and the lean is measured from it, so the rates stay the calibrated ones. No figure for strike, take_in, stay_past_notice, take_from_employer or an organisation's conduct (the survey's items on joining strikes and on the justifiability of stealing property were not opened); no figure by origin group (no source found that gives one). National, not the place's. does_bps is never given: a conduct's own rate in the profile.

Indigenous language speakers (0.8%) and Afro-Mexican self-recognition (1.7%) are also counted by the census but not used here. same_household_bps: 8233 PLACEHOLDER, DERIVED, not a statistic: no table of couples by place of birth was found and opened. It is the chance share of same-group couples from these four groups (sum of squares, 75.6%) raised by the homophily below as c(1+h)/(c(1+h)+1-c) with h=0.5. homophily_bps: PLACEHOLDER 5000 (a close tie is half again as likely within a group as by chance). No survey of close ties or friendship by group for this place was found and opened; McPherson, Smith-Lovin and Cook 2001 ('Birds of a feather', Annual Review of Sociology 27) gives the general fact, not this place's figure. CHILDREN: the census counts a person by their own place of birth, not the parents', so the generator's either-parent rule does not match this source: a child born in Jalisco is born in Jalisco whatever its parents' birthplaces.
sources.tenancy.rent_share_of_income: PLACEHOLDER bands around one opened median: tenant households in Mexico paid a median of 15% of gross income in rent in 2022 (OECD Affordable Housing Database, indicator HC1.2, Housing costs over income, from INEGI's ENIGH 2022, https://oecd.org/els/family/hc1-2-housing-costs-over-income.pdf, opened 2026-10-12; national). No bands were found (ENIGH 2024 by decile, from a news summary and not opened: 32.6% of income in the lowest tenth, 11.5% in the highest). The bands (63% under a fifth, 19% a fifth to three tenths, 13% three tenths to a half, 5% over a half) are a placeholder shaped to that median. To replace from ENIGH's tabulations. HOW IT IS USED (docs/behaviour/generator.md, "Homes by income"): each renting household of a new town draws its share from these bands (evenly within a band; the open band from its lower bound to twice it, at most everything), which gives the rent it carries; households and let homes are matched by it. A target as well: the town's own distribution at the start is reported beside it and is not fitted to it.
sources.support.take_up_bps: pension 90%: PLACEHOLDER: the pension is universal from 65 with no means test (Secretaria de Bienestar, Reglas de Operacion 2024, DOF 29 December 2023, https://www.gob.mx/cms/uploads/attachment/file/878500/PPBPAM2024.pdf, opened 2026-10-12); 13.4 million people were said to receive it in 2026 (a news report of the government's count), and no population of 65 and over was opened to divide by. HOW IT IS USED (docs/behaviour/generator.md, "Payments in force"): of those the payment's rule already entitles as the year begins, this share open with it in payment; the rest claim it when they first look, as before. 2026-10-16: over 926,000 enrolled in the pension in Jalisco (news, 2025) against 686,074 aged 65 and over in the 2020 Census (8.2%, IIEG): enrolment may exceed the 2020 count (different years; women of 63 and 64 are in the phase-in), so 90% looks a floor: not changed (SUMMARY-ONLY).
sources.tenancy.possession: PLACEHOLDERS: the Codigo Civil del Estado de Jalisco lets a landlord rescind a lease for unpaid rent through the civil courts (juicio de desahucio; two months unpaid is the usual ground: recalled, to confirm); no figure was opened. The police stand for the court's actuario. The two shares of how tenants answer are the same in every profile: stay_past_notice_bps 5000 is a PLACEHOLDER (no figure was found for the share of tenants who stay past a notice for arrears); leave_on_order_bps 5900 is England's, used everywhere: of 16,848 landlord possession orders in January to March 2026, 6,888 repossessions were by county court bailiffs, 41%, so about 59% of those ordered out were gone without one (Ministry of Justice, Mortgage and Landlord Possession Statistics, January to March 2026: opened by a research agent for this work, 2026-10-11; a ratio of one quarter's flows, not of one cohort). eviction_notice_days: the notice of the day that whoever carries out a warrant gives the tenant; England's county court bailiffs give 14 days' notice of an eviction (Civil Procedure Rules 83.8A: to confirm, recalled), Germany's Gerichtsvollzieher about three weeks (to confirm); every other place's figure is a PLACEHOLDER (7 days; Ohio 3, within its ten). HOW IT IS USED (docs/behaviour/justice.md, "Possession"): published in the town as a law; a landlord gives a notice to vacate under it, applies to the tribunal if the tenant stays, and asks for a warrant if they stay past its order; the tribunal sets a plan or a date by it; the police carry the warrant out. Tenants who answer, and plans (2026-10-12): answer_bps 4000 is a PLACEHOLDER (no figure was found for this place of how many tenants served with an application for possession answer it in writing or attend; it is the middle of the two figures opened for other places: 43% of hearings with the renter or someone for them in Victoria, 39.3% of tenants present in Cleveland, Ohio). plan_consider 'may' is a PLACEHOLDER: nothing of Jalisco's procedure was opened. 2026-10-16: the Code is now opened (docs.mexico.justia.com copy, arts 1792, 2142, 2144): art 2142 gives the landlord the property back where two or more consecutive months are unpaid AND the property is abandoned, with a court's certification; art 1792: where unpaid rent is the only ground and the tenant pays the arrears and costs before sentence the court must dismiss, and this cannot be waived (so possession for arrears is hard to complete: it is the cure, not modelled as such); art 2144: the landlord may ask for rescission for non-payment. arrears_days 60 fits the two months of art 2142 for abandonment only. notice_days, possession_days, warrant_days and eviction_notice_days are not in the Code text read (the procedure code was not read): still placeholders.
sources.business.entry_bps_per_year: INEGI, Estudio sobre la Demografia de los Negocios 2023: 61 births a month for every 10,000 businesses, 71 deaths (to confirm: read from a search summary, and the window is May 2019 to May 2023, across the pandemic); taken as 7.3% a year. National; Jalisco's own not retrieved. HOW IT IS USED: a target a town's business births are compared with (docs/calibration.md); nothing sets births, which follow expected profit (docs/behaviour/entry.md, "Entry by expected profit"). 2026-10-16: INEGI's Estudio sobre la Demografia de los Negocios 2023 (https://www.inegi.org.mx/contenidos/saladeprensa/aproposito/2024/EAP_MIPYMES24.pdf, opened): births 61 and deaths 71 a month per 10,000 micro, small and medium establishments, May 2019 to May 2023, 61 x 12 = 7.3% a year: the figure agrees; the base is establishments of those sizes, nationally, including reopenings.
sources.employment.hours: Ley Federal del Trabajo arts. 427-430 (art. 427 opened at mley.mx 2026-10-13; arts. 429-430 from search results, to confirm): a temporary suspension of work for economic causes needs the tribunal's authorisation, with an indemnity of up to a month's wage (art. 430), and a reduction of hours is a change of conditions that needs the worker's agreement (arts. 41, 57; not opened). Authorisation by a tribunal is not modelled, so here: firms do not cut hours (they let people go, as before). 48 hours a week: art. 61 (recalled). HOW IT IS USED (docs/behaviour/firms.md, "Hours before heads"): published in the town as a law (law-cutting-hours); a shop or factory over its need cuts everyone's hours to what its trade needs before it lets anyone go, where this says it may, and pays what it owes for the hours cut; a worker reads the employer's paper as the pay agreed. consent_bps 9000 is a PLACEHOLDER (of workers asked to agree to a cut as the alternative to someone being let go, the share who do; no figure found). The employer's own notice of 3 days is ours, so that the paper reaches the worker first. 2026-10-16: opened at mley.mx: art 430: on authorising a suspension for economic cause the tribunal sets an indemnity of at most one month's wage; art 57: either party may ask the tribunal to change conditions where the wage is not remunerative, hours are excessive or economic circumstances justify it (the employer too); art 61: daily hours 8 by day, 7 by night, 7.5 mixed; the page says art 61 was reformed on 1 May 2026, so the weekly total (art 69, not opened) and the step to 46 hours in 2027 are to be rechecked. 'no' holds as a rule that an employer cannot cut hours unilaterally. Jalisco, Q2 2026: mean 41.4 hours a week, 65.0% work 35 to 48, 11.5% over 48 (ENOE, https://www.inegi.org.mx/contenidos/saladeprensa/boletines/2026/enoe/enoe2026_08_Jal.pdf).
sources.employment.adjustment: PLACEHOLDERS, the same in every profile, with a sourced shape (docs/behaviour/firms.md, "Adjusting labour"; docs/research/references.md). smooth_months 3: firms plan production and workforce on smoothed, forecast trade and not on the last period's (Holt, Modigliani, Muth and Simon 1960); no figure for the horizon of a small employer here was found. hiring_cost_weeks 8: what recruiting and training a new worker costs, in weeks of their pay; estimates run from under two weeks to over sixteen (Silva and Toledo 2009; Manning 2011; Blatter, Muehlemann and Schenker 2012; Muehlemann and Leiser 2018: all to confirm, none opened), and none is for this place.
sources.employment.termination: Ley Federal del Trabajo (https://mley.mx/LFT/articulo/48/, /50/, /162/, opened 2026-10-16): art 48: on dismissal without just cause the worker may choose reinstatement or three months' pay, and back wages (salarios vencidos) up to 12 months, then 2% a month interest on the 15 months' pay; art 50: for an indefinite contract 20 days' pay for each year of service on top of the three months (for a fixed term under a year, half the time served); art 162: the seniority premium of 12 days' pay for each year of service, paid also on dismissal, independently of other benefits (capped at twice the minimum wage, arts 485 and 486, not read). No notice period. The table here is the three months plus 32 days a year (20 + 12) of completed service, in steps (years 0, 1 to 5, 7 and 10; the years between take the step below): the premium was added on 2026-10-16, from the 20 days alone; it is overstated for the better paid because the cap on its base is left out (32.3% of Jalisco's employed earn up to one minimum wage and 44.7% one to two, ENOE Q2 2026, so most are under it). Back wages, which would add up to 12 months where the employer loses at the tribunal, are not modelled (no field). Platform workers were added to the Act in December 2024. HOW IT IS USED (docs/behaviour/firms.md, "Adjusting labour"): published in the town as a law; an employer reads it before letting someone go for redundancy (what it would owe is part of what the job costs to end) and pays what it says when the job ends. Service is counted from the start of a run: nobody's earlier years with an employer are known to it.
sources.frictions: Everyday frictions (docs/behaviour/frictions.md): what goes wrong, how often, and how the bodies that hear it work. Read by the generator only for a town whose spec has `living`.
sources.frictions.per_adult_bps_per_year: Of adults, the share who had each kind of problem, a year: half the share who had it in the last two years in World Justice Project, Global Insights on Access to Justice 2019 (General Population Poll 2017-18, about 1,000 respondents a country; the summary statistics workbook was opened; national, and for Brazil and Mexico the three largest cities only). landlord: a problem with a landlord over agreements, payments, repairs, deposits or eviction (0.9% in two years; all of it is given to disrepair here, which overstates repairs: the town has no other landlord problem of the kind yet). wages: difficulty obtaining wages or employment benefits agreed in advance (1.4%). bill: major disruption of a utility's supply or incorrect billing (14.7%; all of it is given to wrong bills). benefits: difficulty obtaining public benefits or government assistance (1.6%). goods: a consumer problem (19.3%) less the utility share, since the survey's consumer problems include it (derived; poor professional services are in it too). The generator turns each into a rate for those exposed (a let dwelling, a job, a customer, a claim) with the town's own counts. Halving a two-year share understates a yearly one where people have a problem in both years (to confirm against a yearly survey). 2026-10-16 (not applied): the Jalisco labour conciliation centre handled 3,956 conciliations in June 2026 (3,730 in June 2025), mostly terminations (1,758) and benefits (515), about 45,000 a year, 73 basis points of persons 15 and over (derived; IIEG, https://iieg.gob.mx/ns/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/ficha_conciliaciones_laborales_jalisco_junio_2026.pdf, opened): a flow of disputes, mostly dismissals, whose benefits-only part is about 10 basis points: the 70 here is not matched. Profeco: the electricity company is the firm most complained of (37,000 complaints in 2021-25), excess charge about half (El Imparcial, 7 April 2026): counts without a denominator, no rate. pay_short_by_bps, bill_over_bps, goods_faulty_share_bps, repair_hours: no figure found.
sources.frictions.put_right_on_asking_bps: Asked to put it right, how often the other side does. PLACEHOLDERS, every one: each stands at the share of people with any problem who say it is done and fully resolved (56.5%: World Justice Project, Global Insights on Access to Justice 2019 (General Population Poll 2017-18, about 1,000 respondents a country; the summary statistics workbook was opened; national, and for Brazil and Mexico the three largest cities only)), which is an outcome of everything people tried, not the rate at which the other side agrees when asked: to replace with a figure by kind of problem. 2026-10-16 (not applied): Profeco conciliated 78% of 89,618 complaints in 2024 and 73% in 2025 (El Imparcial, 6 February 2025, opened; 2025 from a search result): of those who had already escalated, and 'conciliated' may be partial, so not the share who put a thing right when first asked.

sources.frictions.support: (Until foundations F6 this note also gave a processing time, a placeholder fortnight, and a daily capacity; both are gone: how long a claim takes is the hours of whoever decides it.) wrong_refusal_bps: of claims that qualify, the share wrongly refused. FITTED in the 1,000-person town of the first profile (7% of qualifying claims gives about as many refusals a year as 6% of adults, its survey share with difficulty obtaining public benefits, counting the refusals that are right), and for every other place scaled by its own survey share against that one: a stand-in until a place's own rate of decisions changed on review is found. 2026-10-12: this fit assumed every entitled person claims in the year. A town now opens with the payments its people are already entitled to in force (granted before the year, never decided in it), so it decides fewer claims and refuses fewer (Victoria 37.8 to 24.8 a year). It is NOT re-fitted: that would be fitting an outcome again. sources.outlook.residence: PLACEHOLDER: no figure for how long people have lived at their address was found for Mexico on a page opened. Borrowed from Australia's (the only place whose figures were opened), for lack of any: ABS, 2021 Census, 'Population movement in Australia' (released 8 November 2022; abs.gov.au/articles/population-movement-australia), opened 2026-10-11: 53.1% of the population lived at the same address five years before the Census; 14.3% changed address within Australia in the year before; 0.7% had lived overseas a year before. National figures, not Victoria's: the Victoria figures were not found on an opened page. The open band is read as 5 to 15 years by the generator. Mexico's own are probably different (to source: Census or housing-survey tables of years since moving in).
sources.outlook.job_tenure: How long employed people have been with their current employer (starting attachment to the trade). OECD, 'Employment by job tenure intervals' (dataset OECD.ELS.SAE DSD_TENURE@DF_TENURE_FREQ, measure TENURE_EMP, share of employment by time with the current employer; both sexes, all ages), national figures for Mexico, 2025; read from the OECD SDMX API (sdmx.oecd.org/public/rest/data/OECD.ELS.SAE,DSD_TENURE@DF_TENURE_FREQ) on 2026-10-11, the response opened and the figures copied: under 1 year, 1 to under 3, 3 to under 5, 5 to under 10, 10 and over. The open band (10 and over) is read as 10 to 30 years by the generator. The shares sum to 99.9 to 100 in the source and are scaled to 10000.
sources.employment.registered_bps: ILOSTAT (the ILO's SDMX service, sdmx.ilo.org/rest/data/ILO,<dataflow>/<country>.A....?format=csv&startPeriod=2018; each file opened and the figures read from it by a research agent for this work, 2026-10-09), dataflow DF_EMP_NIFL_SEX_STE_RT, Mexico, 2025 (source: ENOE): 43.095% of employees are in informal employment, so 56.9% of employees' jobs are registered. National: the Jalisco bulletin gives no split by position (its labour informality rate for everyone, TIL1, is 46.5% in the 2nd quarter of 2026). HOW IT IS USED (docs/behaviour/firms.md, "Jobs an employer does not register"): each employer of a kind registers this share of its own jobs; a job outside it is paid whole, nothing is withheld and no report names the worker. The same share is given for shops, factories and construction because the source divides employees by status, not by kind of employer (its rates by activity count own-account workers too, and are not used). Nothing inspects: the share is a stated fact of the place. In this profile the only charge on pay is the income tax; the worker's social-security share, which is what registration with the IMSS brings, is not in it (the tax note says so).
sources.employment.own_account: [MIXED] Share: INEGI, Encuesta Nacional de Ocupacion y Empleo (ENOE), Jalisco, segundo trimestre de 2026, bulletin of 25 August 2026, cuadro 3 (https://www.inegi.org.mx/contenidos/saladeprensa/boletines/2026/enoe/enoe2026_08_Jal.pdf; opened and read by a research agent for this work, 2026-10-09): own-account workers (cuenta propia) 16.9% of the employed (647,669 people; employers 7.4%, unpaid 2.2%). sources.currency: Mexican pesos, in centavos: written with the peso sign, which is the same character as the dollar sign ('$1,234.56'; the sign carries no code, so a reader outside Mexico cannot tell pesos from dollars by it), or in words as pesos and centavos. ISO 4217: MXN, two decimal places. Banco de México, https://www.banxico.org.mx (the peso, 'peso mexicano'; the page was not opened: to confirm). In-world the participants simply write '$' as people in Mexico do. How its people write money: the peso sign before the digits with no space, a point before the decimals, commas between thousands (Mexico, unlike most Spanish-speaking countries, uses the English marks). Unicode CLDR (cldr-json, cldr-numbers-full/main/es-MX/numbers.json, opened 2026-10-08): decimal '.', group ',', currency pattern '¤#,##0.00'. Banco de México and the Real Academia's usage were not opened. Both marks are stated so that "$1.234" is read as a decimal with a digit too many.
sources.households: IIEG Jalisco, ficha informativa 'Los hogares censales en Jalisco 2020' (1 March 2022; from INEGI, Censo 2020), https://iieg.gob.mx/ns/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/HogaresCensalesJalisco2020.pdf: of 2,330,706 census households in Jalisco in 2020, 12.6% were one-person (unipersonal), 85.9% family households (nuclear 73.8% of them, extended 25.0%, compound 1.2%) and 0.5% unspecified; non-family households of co-residents were 23,104 (1.0% of all). lone_bps = 1,260 (unipersonal). group_bps = 200: co-residents 1.0% plus compound households 1.2% of family households (about 1.0% of all), counted with groups as the au-vic-2026 profile counts its 'other' families. The remaining 85.4% are family households, of which 22.5% are EXTENDED or compound (more than one family nucleus, or relatives beyond the nucleus). THE STRUCTURE HAS NO EXTENDED HOUSEHOLD, so all family households are assigned to the three nuclear types in proportion to a split of the nuclear type. That split (couple without children 14%, couple with children 70%, one parent 16% of the nuclear and extended family households) is a PLACEHOLDER: the Jalisco split of nuclear households by type was not found. Cross-checks: IIEG Jalisco, same ficha, 68.4% of children under 18 lived with both parents, 20.0% with their mother only, 2.1% with their father only, 3.1% with neither; INEGI (Censo 2020, national) found single-mother households headed by women 9.5% of households (https://www.gaceta.unam.mx/transformacion-compleja-del-concepto-de-familia/ and https://www.aztecajalisco.com/noticias/6-de-marzo-dia-de-la-familia-en-mexico/, secondary reports; not opened). children_couple and children_one_parent (shares of 1, 2, 3+ children at home): placeholders shaped by Jalisco's total fertility of 1.89 (ENADID 2023) and the ENIGH 2024 average of 0.74 members under 15 per household. same_sex_couple_bps: INEGI Censo 2020, national: 1.2% of households have at least one same-sex couple (reported by https://mexicocomovamos.mx/animal-politico/2022/06/sacando-a-las-estadisticas-del-closet-una-mirada-a-la-diversidad-sexual-con-datos-del-censo-2020/ , secondary; not opened; a Jalisco figure and the share of couples were not found: placeholder at 120). lone_parent_female_bps: placeholder (8,600), from single-mother households being the great majority of one-parent households (INEGI Censo 2020, national; exact share not found). adult_female_bps: Censo 2020 Jalisco: 100 women to 96 men overall (51.0% women), more women at older ages, 49.4% of men aged 20-39 (placeholder 51.2%, to confirm against the age and sex table). child_male_bps: Censo 2020 Jalisco, 0-14: 102.2-103.7 boys per 100 girls (about 50.7% boys). mother_age_at_first_birth: placeholder [18, 32] (ENADID 2023 reports age at first birth; the median was not extracted; to confirm). child_max_age 24, adult_ages and group_size: the same simplifications as the au-vic-2026 profile (children at home drawn up to 24; adults 18-99; groups of 2-3), not Mexican figures. (Added 2026-10-08, not by this note's author: the structure now has extended households, and they are taken out of the three nuclear types: see households.extended_bps.)
sources.households.extended_bps: The ficha of `households` (IIEG Jalisco, 'Los hogares censales en Jalisco 2020', from INEGI, Censo 2020, as that note cites it): 25.0% of family households are extended, and family households are 85.9% of all, so 21.475% of all households, 2,148 in 10,000. Compound households (1.2% of family households) stay with groups, where the author put them. Until 2026-10-08 the profile had no such kind and its author spread the extended households over the three nuclear types by a split of 14%, 70% and 16%; they are taken out in the same proportions (couple_bps 1,196 to 895, couple_children_bps 5,978 to 4,474, one_parent_bps 1,366 to 1,023: together 6,392, the author's 8,540 less 2,148). That split is still the author's PLACEHOLDER. Not in the ficha as the author read it, so not stated here and left to the generator's rule: the family an extended household is built around (drawn by the same three shares, which is what the author's spreading assumed) and who the relatives are (one other adult relative, the least that makes a household extended). To replace with INEGI's tabulation of extended households by kinship to the head. Not re-opened when this was added: the figures are those the author's note records.
sources.households.age_bands_bps: INEGI, Censo de Población y Vivienda 2020, Presentación de resultados, Jalisco, https://www.inegi.org.mx/contenidos/programas/ccpv/2020/doc/cpv2020_pres_res_jal.pdf, 'Estructura de la población, 2000, 2010 y 2020' (median age 29): percentage of the population by five-year age group, men and women added (0-4: 4.1+4.0, 5-9: 4.4+4.3, ... 85 and over 0.3+0.5; the two pyramids sum to 100.0%); 85 and over taken to 99. sources.life.qx_per_100000: PLACEHOLDER MODEL TABLE: no single-year life table by sex for Jalisco was found (CONAPO publishes projections of e0 and mortality, not the full table, on the pages opened). A Heligman-Pollard-shaped curve (infant, young-adult hump with a larger hump for men, senescent rise), fitted by bisection so that life expectancy at birth matches CONAPO's projection for Jalisco in 2024: men 73.00 years, women 79.28 years, and infant mortality matches CONAPO's 2023 figures for Jalisco (10.04 per 1,000 boys, 8.29 per 1,000 girls). The shape between 1 and 100 is the model's, not an observed table: replace with the CONAPO or INEGI abridged table by sex for Jalisco (INEGI mortality statistics, deaths registered, give the ages at death) when found. The fit gives male qx at 20 of 167 per 100,000, which is plausible for a country with high male violent mortality but unverified.

Carried over from au-vic-2026's percentiles and scaled by the ratio of the two profiles' shop wages (2.50 pesos per Australian dollar), which assumes Mexican balances relative to wages match Australian ones: surely too high for Mexico, where many adults have no bank account.
